1.pericope_label: He made the altar of burnt offering

schools.summary: Make the transition itself carry a lesson. The gold work, though the richest of all that was made, had been ordered to lie most out of sight within the tabernacle; what is described now stands open to the view of everyone, and both pieces of it are of brass. Then state the altar's office plainly, since everything else rests on it: all their sacrifices were offered there, and the altar, being itself sanctified for that purpose by divine appointment, sanctified the gift that was offered upon it in faith. From that pass directly to the use. Christ was himself the altar to his own sacrifice of atonement, and he is so to all our sacrifices of acknowledgment; we must have an eye to him in offering them, as God has in accepting them.

Notice first what is easy to miss in a chapter that repeats an earlier one: the purport is the same as before, with the order of some parts transposed, though not a word is changed. Then give the reason the specification was so exact. The altar was made of the materials and in the form God had prescribed, so that the people might bring their sacrifices for the expiation of sin and for thanksgiving with the surer confidence, knowing the thing was as he had appointed it. And settle a small question the text raises by its wording: the making is ascribed to Bezaleel though the work was plainly not done by one pair of hands, because he had the care and oversight of it and it was made by his direction. The account of the altar, its horns, vessels, rings and staves is then carried on through the verses that follow.

Set the chapter's contents out at its head, so the reader knows what is coming: the altar of burnt offering first, then the laver and its foot made from the mirrors, then the court with its pillars and hangings, then the whole work finished by Bezaleel and Aholiab with their assistants, and last the amounts of gold, silver and brass and how each was expended. On the altar itself, refer back to the chapter where it was first commanded and where the Hebrew terms for its horns, pots, shovels and basins are explained, since this chapter records execution rather than instruction. Then take the typical sense in one stroke: Christ was himself the altar to his own sacrifice of atonement, and so he is to all our sacrifices of acknowledgment; we must have an eye to him in offering them, as God has in accepting them.

Mark the turn the narrative takes and let the structure do the explaining. Having finished with the furniture of the sanctuary, the account moves outward to the furniture of the court in which the sanctuary stood; and that court held two things, the brazen altar and the great laver. The construction of the first is related in the verses immediately following, and that of the second in the verse after them. Keep the reader oriented in the sequence rather than pausing over what has already been described at length elsewhere.

debates.question: What is the point of repeating what was already commanded?

The transition is structural: from the furniture of the sanctuary to the furniture of the court, which held the brazen altar and the great laver

This chapter records execution rather than instruction, so the terms themselves belong to the earlier place where they were explained

8.pericope_label: The laver of brass, of the looking glasses of the women; the court

schools.summary: Correct the translation before anything else, because the received English makes nonsense of the verse. The Hebrew word means a reflector of any kind, and what is meant must be highly polished metal, since glass was not yet in use -- and had it been, looking-glasses could not have furnished a brazen laver. Render it mirrors. Then give the history of the object, since it is not obvious to a modern reader: the earliest mirrors were the still fountain and the unruffled lake, then mica, which splits into leaves so fine that a plate with something black behind it reflects well and serves in northern ships for window glass; artificial mirrors began in brass, passed to polished steel, and reached silver as luxury grew, though the earliest were of tin and copper mixed, the best made at Brundusium. On the women, take the notice as honour paid them: they were eminent for devotion and attended public worship more constantly than others. And on what became of their gift, give both possibilities and prefer the second -- either the mirrors were artfully joined together, or melted and cast anew; but more likely the laver was burnished so brightly that its sides still served as mirrors, so that priests coming to wash might see their faces and discover the spots they came to cleanse.

Read the court as a picture of the church under the older covenant. Its walls were hangings like the rest, and they show a garden enclosed, the worshippers confined to a little compass; but the enclosure being of curtains only intimated that the confinement of the church to one particular nation was not to be perpetual, the dispensation itself being movable and mutable, in due time to be taken down and folded up when the place of the tent should be enlarged and its cords lengthened to make room for the Gentile world. Then carry it forward. The church here on earth is but the court of God's house, and those who tread these courts are passing through them to the holy place above. And take the arrangement as instruction in approach: the enclosing of a court before the tabernacle teaches a gradual coming to God, since the priests who ministered had to pass through the holy court before they entered the holy house, so that before solemn ordinances there ought to be a separated court of solemn preparation, in which we wash our hands and so draw near with a true heart.

Identify the objects exactly. Brass here means bronze; and the mirrors of the ancient world were not glass but burnished metal, bronze being the metal ordinarily used and in common use in Egypt, where they took the form of round or oval plates with a handle, much like a fire-screen; Etruscan women used the same articles, often delicately chased with engravings. Then say what the women did and what was done with it. These were the women accustomed to frequent the tent of meeting recently set up, and to flock thither in troops; they offered voluntarily, for the service of God, articles that were among the most highly prized of their possessions. Moses marked his approval of their devotion by forming those offerings into the most honourable of all the brazen vessels, and by recording the fact to the women's credit.

Keep the account of the metals straight, since the text distinguishes what a casual reading runs together. The laver was not made from the brass of the offering: out of that were made the brazen altar with its grate and vessels, the sockets of the court and of the court gate, and the pins of the tabernacle, and the laver is nowhere named among them. It was made, as this verse says, from the mirrors. For the court itself, with its pillars, sockets, hangings, hooks and pins, refer the reader to the place where each was first described rather than repeating the detail here.

sides.position: Either they were artfully joined together or melted down and cast anew; but more likely the laver was burnished so brightly that its sides still served as mirrors, so priests coming to wash might see their faces and discover the spots

21.pericope_label: The sum of the tabernacle; the gold, the silver and the brass reckoned

schools.summary: Do not quote a money value until the system behind it has been laid out. The ancients reckoned by talents subdivided into minas and drachms, and the Hebrews had besides their shekels and half-shekels; the text itself fixes the talent, since six hundred and three thousand five hundred and fifty men at half a shekel each yield a sum that proves a talent contained three thousand shekels. Settle the shekel's value before converting anything, and say openly that authorities differ. Then ask the question the amounts really raise, which is why so much wealth was demanded at all, and give three reasons. To impress the people with the dignity of the divine majesty and the importance of his service. To take out of their hands riches they had no use for in the wilderness, where they were miraculously supported, and which might otherwise have engendered the love that is the root of all evil. And to check pride, by leading them to give up even the ornaments of their persons, which would have diverted their minds from better things. Add the public inference the contribution suggests: gold raised by voluntary offering and silver by tribute show that either way may be taken for defraying public expenses, provided nothing be done with partiality.

Begin with the words. Report the renderings offered for the opening phrase -- these are the accounts, this is the reckoning -- and correct the clause that follows, which is not for the service of the Levites but a service of the Levites, rendered by the hand of Ithamar. Remove the mistranslation in the description of the second workman, since the word rendered engraver means a worker in any material whatever and should be artificer, while cunning workman is literally a deviser, the root being used especially of devising textile fabrics. Then handle the sums honestly. Give the competing estimates for the gold rather than one figure, and say that on any of them the amount is remarkable, showing both the liberal spirit of the people and a general sense that the occasion required lavish expenditure; note too that there is no difficulty in supposing they possessed it, having carried a vast quantity of ornaments out of Egypt. Observe that the silver named is only the atonement-money of those numbered, not the freewill silver, and that the hundred talents cast one to a socket account exactly for the ninety-six sockets of the boards and the four of the pillars.

Say what the inventory is for, since it is not architecture. The reference here is not so much to the fabric of the tabernacle as to its perpetual conservation: its several parts were numerically distinguished and consigned as it were to registers, and deposited by Ithamar with the Levites, so that they might know what they had in charge and no part of it be lost. Take the reckoning also as a testimony about the men who handled it. The whole work was divine, both because Moses faithfully delivered the commands of God and because the artificers followed them with precise accuracy; and from the counting up of the gold and silver and the showing of what each was spent upon, we gather that every one honestly discharged his duty, that none was corrupted or drawn aside by covetousness so as to fall from his integrity, and that the entire sum was collected and paid without fraud. Then keep the small explanations exact: the half-shekel is named from a root meaning to divide, the hundred talents of silver formed the sockets that were the silver foundation of the whole fabric, and the brass may well have come from the neighbouring mountains of Arabia.

Set out the procedure as an audit, because that is what it was. Bezaleel and Aholiab brought in the account, Ithamar drew it up and gave it in to Moses, and the young priest was by these lesser services trained up and fitted for greater. Then distinguish the two kinds of contribution and let the contrast stand. All the gold was a freewill offering, every man bringing as he could and would, and of it were made the golden furniture and vessels. The silver was levied by way of tax, every man assessed at half a shekel, a kind of poll-money; and of that they made the sockets into which the boards of the tabernacle were let and on which they rested. Give the totals as they stand in the text, with a plain estimate of their present worth, and leave the reader to weigh what such an expenditure implied.

debates.question: Why is an audited reckoning part of the record?

sides.position: For conservation, not architecture: the parts were consigned as it were to registers and deposited with the Levites so they should know their charge and nothing be lost; and the counting shows none was drawn aside by covetousness
As an audit: Bezaleel and Aholiab brought in the account, Ithamar drew it up and gave it to Moses, and the young priest was by lesser services trained for greater
As accounts or a reckoning, rendered by the hand of Ithamar; the phrase recurs elsewhere in the Pentateuch
As a detail of everything the two workmen had been commanded to make, reckoned up by the Levites under Ithamar

Three estimates for the gold, from nearly three hundred and twenty thousand pounds down to a hundred and thirty-two thousand; on any of them the amount is remarkable, and the people plainly had it from what they carried out of Egypt
Something near the lowest of those figures, on a shekel valued at ten thalers
About a hundred and fifty thousand pounds worth of gold at present value
No figure can be given until the whole system of ancient reckoning is laid out and the value of the shekel settled, on which authorities differ

debates.question: What follows from gold being freely given and silver assessed?

sides.position: That either way may be taken for defraying public expenses, provided nothing be done with partiality
That compulsory payment toward the sanctuary was sanctioned at the very moment when voluntary offering was most praised, so that church rates are defensible in principle from both Testaments
The contrast is simply recorded: gold as every man could and would, silver as a kind of poll-money
The question to ask is not how it was raised but why so much was required -- to impress the divine majesty, to remove riches that might have bred covetousness, and to check pride

outliers.note: Alone draws a question of church finance out of the assessment, calling it remarkable that compulsory payment toward the sanctuary should be sanctioned at the very time when the greatest stress was laid on the acceptableness of voluntary offerings, and concluding that church rates are defensible in principle from both Testaments.

Alone asks why so much wealth was demanded at all and answers with three reasons -- to impress the dignity of the divine majesty, to take out of the people's hands riches they had no use for in the wilderness and which might have bred the love that is the root of all evil, and to check pride by making them surrender even the ornaments of their persons.
